clusters.text: Ambulances lined up outside Wainwright Health Centre after the deadly blast at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Several people have been killed or injured as a result of a large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta, the nation's defence minister has said. David McGuinty did not confirm the cause or the number of casualties, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate". The Canadian military and local authorities were managing the fire, he said. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases. Canadian TV network Global News reported that at least seven were killed and dozens more injured when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding that his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected". The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation said Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton had called a code orange, a disaster response protocol for responding to a high-casualty incident. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor there, told the broadcaster that the number of patients would otherwise "overwhelm" Edmonton's healthcare facilities. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster." Defence Minister David McGuinty did not specify how many had died in the fire After the fire erupted on Saturday, it "spread rapidly due to high winds" and had torn through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said. The defence minister told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory". It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT). Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In the French capital, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC that they were "pacifists" who were "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". clusters.text: At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say. The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter. West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families. A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.". Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions. Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

clusters.text: Japanese space agency leading five-year mission to Phobos, one of ‘most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system’ Japan is to launch a spacecraft on the world’s first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars. Scientists hope the mission, which is expected to take five years, will provide clues to how Phobos and its smaller sibling Deimos formed, and hopefully even shed light on the origins of life in the solar system. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) is aiming to launch the spacecraft on Tuesday on a new Japanese mainstay H3 rocket. Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager for the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, said samples from Phobos would provide useful data for scientists to consider using a Martian moon as a base for a future manned mission to the planet. The US, China and others are hoping to send astronauts to Mars . “Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated,” Kawakatsu said. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system.” Japan is leading an international mission, which includes equipment and communications support from Nasa and other national space agencies. Since the 1960s, dozens of missions have been sent to Mars, but its moons largely remain a mystery. Multiple Russian attempts to land on Phobos, including one launched in 2011, have failed. Phobos and Deimos take their names from the Greek mythological personifications of fear and terror, sons of the war god Ares, whose Roman counterpart is Mars. A key question is how they formed and what they are made of. Some scientists think the two irregular crater-pocked bodies could be remnants of debris formed after a large celestial object crashed into Mars. Others say the moons could be asteroids that have come from elsewhere. Jaxa officials think samples from Phobos will provide answers. “We can almost certainly come to a conclusion by analysing soil samples,” said Kiyoshi Kuramoto, principal investigator on the mission. Scientists chose to collect samples from Phobos mainly because the moon is closer to Mars than Deimos, and therefore may have more information about the planet. clusters.text: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung. The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers. The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery. On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation. The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced. The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace". It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion. The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive. The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world. Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years. It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment. clusters.text: The US secretary of state is skipping New Delhi on his second trip to India in six months, and opposition leaders say the arrangements are humiliating. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to visit India in the coming week, but he will not set foot in the capital, New Delhi. Instead, on Monday, Rubio will hold talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, and then visit an oil refinery in Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat, according to a statement from the US Department of State. His itinerary sparked a political storm after the US ambassador to India said Washington expected Jaishankar to travel to meet Rubio, prompting opposition leaders to accuse the government of allowing India’s top diplomat to be “summoned” on home soil. The spat comes as relations between the two countries are strained over trade, tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil. So why is Rubio avoiding New Delhi, and why has it caused such upset? Here’s what you need to know: Rubio is arriving on Sunday from Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he has been meeting with five Central Asian states at the C5+1 summit . In India, he is due to meet senior officials to discuss the US-India strategic partnership and energy cooperation and hold talks with business leaders, the State Department said. Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal appeared to confirm the agenda, stating on Friday that the Mumbai talks would cover energy, trade and investment, defence, and critical and emerging technologies. In Jamnagar, Rubio is to visit the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, and attend a reception hosted by the Ambani family, according to The Hindu newspaper. Rubio was in the Indian capital in May for a meeting of foreign ministers of countries in the Quad, a group consisting of the US, India, Japan and Australia. The State Department has framed his upcoming trip around energy and investment, and the second stop on Rubio’s India visit, Jamnagar, is one of the world’s most important energy hubs. The visit also comes as fuel prices bite in the US before next month’s midterm elections. clusters.title: Early Menopause Is A Growing Indian Problem: What Working Women Are Missing
clusters.text: For a woman in her late thirties, irregular periods may seem like a consequence of work stress, while disturbed sleep, anxiety, exhaustion and difficulty concentrating are easily blamed on demanding schedules or family responsibilities. But these changes can sometimes signal perimenopause, the transition leading up to menopause, which may begin years before menstruation stops. "Indian women reach menopause years earlier than women in most of the world. The average age here is around 46 to 47," says Dr Anjana Singh, Director of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Fortis Hospital, Noida . For working women, she points out, this means menopause can arrive in the middle of their careers rather than near retirement. Indian research reinforces the need for greater awareness. An analysis of National Family Health Survey-5 ( NFHS-5 ) data found that 5.5% of currently married women aged 35-39 were classified as being in menopause . Although this does not establish that menopause is becoming more common, it highlights how early the transition may be relevant. "Perhaps the biggest gap is awareness. Women have been taught to plan for periods, pregnancy and contraception. We have done far less to prepare them for the decades that follow," says Dr Kanika Batra Modi, Director and Clinical Lead, Gynae Onco, Max Hospital, Saket . Early Menopause: Why Women in Their 30s May Miss the Signs Perimenopause can begin several years before the final menstrual period. Symptoms may include irregular or changing menstrual cycles, hot flushes, night sweats, disturbed sleep, mood changes, anxiety, brain fog, joint pain and low energy. Vaginal dryness and urinary symptoms may also develop. "Busy women blame deadlines, commutes or parenting, and keep going," says Dr Singh, explaining why the transition can go unrecognised. Workplace stigma adds another barrier, with women sometimes reluctant to discuss symptoms for fear of being perceived as less capable. Dr Modi notes that menstrual changes and exhaustion are frequently normalised during some of the busiest professional and personal years. However, these symptoms should not automatically be attributed to menopause. Pregnancy, thyroid disorders and other medical or hormonal conditions can also affect menstrual cycles and energy levels. clusters.snippet: Britain's Sonay Kartal beats former French Open winner Jelena Ostapenko to reach the Wuhan Open final in only her third event after a six-month injury lay-off.
clusters.text: Sonay Kartal is the first British player to reach a WTA 1,000 final since Johanna Konta in 2019 Sonay Kartal's dream week continued as she beat former Grand Slam champion Jelena Ostapenko at the Wuhan Open to reach the biggest final of her career. British number five Kartal is playing in only her third event since returning from a six-month absence with a back injury, but she now stands one more victory away from a WTA 1,000 title - one of the most prestigious prizes outside of the Grand Slams. The 24-year-old's composure helped her secure a 7-6 (11-9) 7-6 (7-5) victory in a pulsating semi-final against Latvia's Ostapenko. Kartal trailed 4-1 in both sets but remained level-headed and took advantage when 34th-ranked Ostapenko stuttered in high-pressure moments. Remarkably, Kartal survived three set points in the first set, and three more set points in the second, to secure a victory which will long live in the memory. "That was probably one of the toughest matches I've ever played," said Kartal. "At times she is unplayable and you have to ride that wave. Mentally, this is one of the best performances of my career." The world number 170 is the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1,000 final since the format was introduced in 1990. Kartal will play French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska - who beat six-time major champion Iga Swiatek in their semi-final - for the title on Sunday. Reaching the final means Kartal, who has been as high as 44th in the world, will return to the world's top 50 and become Britain's number one player when the next rankings are released on Monday. clusters.title: PDA plans action against Atiq Ahmed’s wife Shaista’s plot in Prayagraj | Hindustan Times
clusters.text: The Prayagraj Development Authority (PDA) is preparing to act against a plot of around one acre near Airavat Crossing, reportedly owned by absconding Shaista Parveen, wife of slain gangster-politician Atiq Ahmed, officials said on Saturday.The proposed action follows chief minister Yogi Adityanath performing the bhoomi pujan for a housing project on land freed from Atiq’s alleged encroachment in Kasari-Masari on Thursday. Earlier, a housing project for economically weaker sections was developed on land freed in Lukerganj, where flats were allotted to poor families.Officials said the two projects were part of a wider exercise to identify properties allegedly linked to Atiq, his brother Ashraf and Shaista. The PDA has sought details of plots registered in their names from the registration department. Further action will follow the examination of records and original property documents, officials added.According to district authorities, Atiq had allegedly occupied land in several localities, including Kareli, Karbala, Ghauspur-Katuhla, Karaibagh, Niva and Kasari-Masari. The authority is now widening its scrutiny to cover assets linked to other family members.The family is also reported to have substantial landholdings around Prayagraj airport. Following preliminary inputs, the PDA has written to the land registration department, asking it not to register sale deeds for identified plots, officials said.Officials have not publicly disclosed details of the properties. However, prospective buyers seeking information are reportedly being cautioned about the disputed status of the land to prevent investment in potentially contentious transactions.“The campaign against illegally acquired assets will continue. Action will also be taken against a plot in Shaista’s name near Airavat Crossing. We will not allow any land mafia to become active. The work will be carried out in accordance with the state government’s zero-tolerance policy,” said Rishi Raj, PDA vice-chairman.The authority said the broader objective was to prevent illegal land occupation and make land freed from encroachments available for housing for economically weaker sections.
